1. What is Reinforcement Learning? Reinforcement Learning (RL), at its core, is a method of learning. Learning based on wikipedia, is the process of acquiring new understanding and knowledge. To simplify it: when you see something, you know something more than that.
Some classic ways of learning can be shown as examples.
In supervised learning, we learn from supervised examples:
$$ \text{input} \rightarrow \text{target} $$
The model sees an input and is taught what the correct corresponding target should be. If we later see a different input with the same label, we learn to associate it with the same target.
In unsupervised learning, we are not given explicit labels. Instead, the model tries to discover hidden structures, patterns, or relationships within the data by itself. Reinforcement Learning is different. In RL, an agent learns by interacting with an environment. It takes actions, observes the consequences, receives rewards, which are not necessarily just numbers, and gradually reinforces its behavior toward directions that may lead to higher long-term return.
So RL is not only about one-step causal reasoning. It is about training a policy and developing an understanding of value. A policy answers:
$$ \text{What should I do?} $$
A value function answers:
$$ \text{How good is this situation, if I keep behaving like this?} $$
2. Markov Assumption and Policy Forms When studying RL, we usually begin with an important assumption: the environment satisfies the Markov property.
$$ P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, \dots)= P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) $$
This means that, given the current state and action, the next state no longer depends on the entire past history.
In other words, the current state is assumed to contain all the information needed for predicting the future.
Under this assumption, we can define two broad forms of policies.
A Markov policy only depends on the current state:
$$ \pi_\theta(a \mid s): \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \Delta(\mathcal{A}) $$
A more general history-dependent policy may depend on the full trajectory so far:
$$ \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_{1:t}, a_{1:t-1}) $$
In principle, a general policy has more information. It can look at the whole past. But in a Markov environment, the current state already summarizes the useful part of the past.
The goal of both policies is the same: maximize the expected return from the initial state.
$$ \max_\pi V^\pi(s_1) $$
3. Why is a Markov Policy Enough? A beautiful result in RL says that, in a Markov environment, we do not lose optimality by restricting ourselves to Markov policies.
More formally, for any history-dependent policy $\pi$, there exists a Markov policy $\mu$ such that
$$ V^{\pi}(s_1) \leq V^\mu(s_1) $$
The intuition is simple.
If the state really contains all information needed for future prediction, then the agent does not need to remember the entire past. At each state, it only needs to choose an action that leads to the best possible future.
So the optimal decision can be made from the current state alone.
This is one of the reasons why Markov Decision Processes are so central in RL. They give us a clean mathematical world where memory can be replaced by state [3].
4. How Do We Know Whether a Policy is Good? In RL, the objective is special: what we optimize is also how we measure success. The goal itself becomes the metric — accumulated reward.
If a policy achieves a higher return, we call it better.
In a finite-horizon setting, the value function is defined as
$$ V_h^\pi(s)= E_{\pi} \left[ \sum_{\tau=h}^{H} r(s_{\tau}, a_{\tau}) \mid s_h = s \right] $$
It means: starting from state $s$ at time $h$, if we follow policy $\pi$, what total reward do we expect to collect until the end?
The action-value function, or Q-function, also conditions on the first action:
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= E_\pi \left[ \sum_{h’=h}^{H} r(s_{h’}, a_{h’}) \mid s_h = s, a_h = a \right] $$
So $V^\pi$ tells us how good a state is, while $Q^\pi$ tells us how good a state-action pair is.
This small difference is extremely important. Once we know $Q^\pi(s,a)$, action selection becomes easier: we can compare actions directly.
5. Monte Carlo Estimation of Value One natural way to estimate value is very direct: start from a state, roll out the policy many times, and average the returns.
This is the Monte Carlo idea [1].
$$ V^\pi(s) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( \sum_{h=1}^{H} r(s_h, a_h) \right)_i $$
Here, $N$ is the number of sampled episodes, and $H$ is the horizon length.
Monte Carlo estimation is conceptually clean. If we sample enough trajectories, the average return becomes a good estimate of the true value.
But the problem is variance.
To see this, consider a simplified infinite-horizon discounted return:
$$ G = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_t $$
Assume the rewards are independent and identically distributed:
$$ r_t \sim \mathcal{D}, \qquad E[r_t] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(r_t) = \sigma^2 $$
Then the variance of the return is
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(G) &= \mathrm{Var} \left( \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_t \right) &= \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{2t} \mathrm{Var}(r_t) &= \sigma^2 \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} (\gamma^2)^t &= \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\gamma^2} \end{aligned} $$
When $\gamma$ approaches 1, the horizon becomes effectively long. Since
$$ 1-\gamma^2= (1-\gamma)(1+\gamma) \approx 2(1-\gamma) $$
we get
$$ \mathrm{Var}(G) \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{2(1-\gamma)} $$
This shows why Monte Carlo methods can be noisy in long-horizon problems. The longer the effective horizon, the more future randomness is accumulated into the return estimate.
Also, in real scenarios, rewards are rarely i.i.d. The reward at one step is often related to what happened before and what will happen next, so the randomness does not simply average out. This makes estimating return even more unstable.
6. Bellman Equation: Computing Value Recursively The Bellman equation gives another way to compute value recursively, and is the core idea behind dynamic programming in sequential decision problems [2].
Instead of waiting until the end of the episode, it breaks the return into two parts:
the immediate reward; the value of the next state. For a fixed policy $\pi$, the expectation Bellman equation is
$$ V_h^\pi(s)= \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) Q_h^\pi(s,a) $$
and
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= r_h(s,a) + E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] $$
This is the central recursive idea in RL.
A value is not estimated only by rolling out to the end. It can also be estimated by looking one step ahead and bootstrapping from another value estimate.
In the infinite-horizon discounted case, a typical one-step TD target is
$$ Q(s_t,a_t)= r_t + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) $$
Compared with Monte Carlo, this target depends only on the immediate reward and the estimated value of the next state-action pair.
Its randomness mainly comes from two sources:
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var} \left( r_t + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) \right) &= \mathrm{Var}(r_t) + \gamma^2 \mathrm{Var}_{s’ \sim P} \left( Q(s’,a’) \right) \end{aligned} $$
This is often much lower variance than summing rewards over a long trajectory.
But this lower variance is not free.
7. What Does Bellman Bootstrapping Sacrifice? Monte Carlo estimation is unbiased in the sense that, if we sample complete trajectories, the expected return equals the true value:
$$ E[G_t] = V^\pi(s_t) $$
Bellman-style methods use bootstrapping. The target depends on the current estimate of the value function.
For example, if we use a parameterized Q-function $Q_\theta$, then the target itself contains $Q_\theta$:
$$ r_t + \gamma Q_\theta(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) $$
This introduces bias, especially early in training when $Q_\theta$ is inaccurate.
So there is a classic trade-off:
$$ \text{Monte Carlo: low bias, high variance} $$
$$ \text{Bellman / TD: higher bias during learning, lower variance} $$
A large part of RL algorithm design can be understood as navigating this trade-off.
8. Convergence of the Bellman Equation Since Bellman methods rely on their own current estimates, a natural question appears:
Why should this process converge?
To answer this, we need the idea of a fixed point.
For optimal control, the Bellman optimality equation is
$$ V_h(s)= \max_a Q_h(s,a) $$
with
$$ Q_h(s,a)= r_h(s,a) + \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V*{h+1}(s’) \right] $$
The expectation Bellman equation evaluates a fixed policy. The optimality Bellman equation searches for the best policy.
This reflects a deep duality in RL:
policy evaluation asks: how good is this policy? policy optimization asks: how good can we possibly be? To study convergence, define the Bellman optimality operator $\mathcal{T}$:
$$ (\mathcal{T}V)(s)= \max_a \left( r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) V(s’) \right) $$
Then solving the Bellman equation is equivalent to finding a fixed point:
$$ V = \mathcal{T}V $$
8.1 Banach Fixed Point Theorem The mathematical tool behind this convergence story is the Banach Fixed Point Theorem [4].
Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space. Suppose $\mathcal{T}: X \rightarrow X$ is a contraction mapping, meaning that for some $0 \leq \gamma < 1$,
$$ d(\mathcal{T}u, \mathcal{T}v) \leq \gamma d(u,v), \qquad \forall u,v \in X $$
Then three things hold.
First, $\mathcal{T}$ has a unique fixed point $V^*$:
$$ \mathcal{T}V^* = V^* $$
Second, starting from any initial guess $V_0$, the sequence
$$ V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T}V_k $$
converges to $V^*$.
Third, the error decreases geometrically. For example, an a priori bound is
$$ d(V_k, V^*) \leq \frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma} d(V_1,V_0) $$
and an a posteriori bound is
$$ d(V_k,V^*) \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} d(V_k,V_{k-1}) $$
This theorem gives the formal backbone of value iteration [1, 3].
8.2 Why is the Bellman Operator a Contraction? We can prove that the Bellman optimality operator shrinks the distance between any two value functions.
Using the infinity norm,
$$ \lVert V-U \rVert_\infty= \max_s |V(s)-U(s)| $$
we have
$$ \begin{aligned} \left| {T}V - {T}U \right|_\infty &= \max_s \left| ({T}V)(s)- ({T}U)(s) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &= \max_s \left| \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V(s’) \right] \right)- \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ U(s’) \right] \right) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &\leq \max_s \max_a \left| \gamma \operatorname{E}_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V(s’) - U(s’) \right] \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &= \gamma \max_s \max_a \left| \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) \left( V(s’) - U(s’) \right) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &\leq \gamma \max_s \max_a \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) \left| V(s’) - U(s’) \right| \ &\leq \gamma \left| V-U \right|_\infty . \end{aligned} $$ Because $\gamma < 1$, the Bellman operator is a contraction mapping.
Therefore, by the Banach Fixed Point Theorem, value iteration converges to the unique fixed point $V^*$.
This is one of the most elegant results in RL: a simple recursive update can be guaranteed to converge, not because of magic, but because each Bellman update pulls value estimates closer together.
References [1] Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd edition, MIT Press, 2018.
*Available online: http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html
[2] Richard Bellman. Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press, 1957.
[3] Martin L. Puterman. Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming. Wiley, 1994.
[4] Stefan Banach. “Sur les opérations dans les ensembles abstraits et leur application aux équations intégrales.” Fundamenta Mathematicae, 3:133–181, 1922.

Preface In the previous note, we introduced the basic idea of Reinforcement Learning and discussed how the Bellman equation can be used to compute the value function.
Intuitively, the value function tells us how much future return we can expect from a state, or from taking a particular action in that state.
In this section, we go one step further.
If value tells us how good something is, then a natural question is:
$$ \text{How can we use value to improve the policy?} $$
In other words, we now move from policy evaluation to policy optimization.
1. Bellman Optimality Equation Leads to the Optimal Policy Earlier, we used the Bellman equation to compute value under a fixed policy.
Now we want to use the Bellman optimality equation as a training goal. But before doing that, we should first ask:
$$ \text{If we solve the Bellman optimality equation, can it really give us the optimal policy?} $$
For a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process, we want to prove that
$$ V_h^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_h^\pi(s), \qquad \forall h,s $$
The proof can be understood by backward induction.
Assume that at time $h+1$, the optimal value is already correct:
$$ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_{h+1}^\pi(s), \qquad \forall s $$
We want to show that this also holds at time $h$.
At the terminal step, the agent receives no future reward after the horizon, so
$$ V_{H+1}^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_{H+1}^\pi(s)=0 $$
This gives the base case.
Now consider the action-value function. For any state-action pair $(s,a)$,
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] $$
Taking the maximum over policies gives
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_\pi \left( r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] \right) &= r_h(s,a)+ \max_\pi E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] \end{aligned} $$
By the induction assumption, the optimal continuation value at time $h+1$ satisfies
$$ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s’)= \max_\pi V_{h+1}^\pi(s’), \qquad \forall s' $$
Since a policy can choose actions based on the state it reaches, the optimal continuation policy can be used for every possible next state $s’$. Therefore,
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s’) \right] &= Q_h^{\pi^\star}(s,a) \end{aligned} $$
Now we convert from $Q$ to $V$.
For a stochastic policy, $V_h^\pi(s)$ is an expectation over actions. But the optimal policy can put all probability mass on the best action. Therefore,
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi V_h^\pi(s) &= \max_\pi \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_a \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_a Q_h^{\pi^\star}(s,a) &= V_h^{\pi^\star}(s) \end{aligned} $$
So by backward induction,
$$ V_h^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_h^\pi(s), \qquad \forall h,s $$
The whole point is simple:
If the future value is already optimal, then choosing the action that leads to the best future gives the optimal value now.
2. Solving the Problem by Planning Now we know that if the optimal value function is known, then the optimal policy can be recovered by choosing the action with the highest value.
This gives us a direct solution method: planning.
In the planning setting, we assume the environment model is known:
$$ \text{Env}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,P) $$
That means we know both the reward function $r$ and the transition probability $P$.
The goal is then:
$$ \text{given } r \text{ and } P,\quad \text{compute } \pi^\star $$
This is often called the simulation setting or model-based planning setting.
There are two classical ways to do this.
2.1 Value Iteration Value iteration directly applies the Bellman optimality equation.
For a finite-horizon MDP, initialize
$$ V_{H+1}^\star(s)=0 $$
Then for
$$ h=H,H-1,\dots,0 $$
we compute
$$ Q_h^\star(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ (P_hV_{h+1}^\star)(s,a), \qquad \forall s,a $$
where
$$ (P_hV_{h+1}^\star)(s,a)= E_{s’\sim P_h(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\star(s’) \right] $$
Then update
$$ V_h^\star(s)=\max_a Q_h^\star(s,a) $$
After computing the optimal value, the optimal policy is obtained by
$$ \pi_h^\star(s)= \arg\max_a Q_h^\star(s,a) $$
Intuitively, value iteration works backward in time:
$$ \text{future value}\rightarrow\text{current value}\rightarrow\text{current action} $$
It builds a global value map first, and then uses this value map to guide the actor.
2.2 Policy Iteration Policy iteration takes another view.
Instead of directly updating the value toward the optimal Bellman equation, it alternates between two steps:
evaluate the current policy; improve the policy using the current value. Initialize an arbitrary policy:
$$ \pi^0 $$
At iteration $t$, first do policy evaluation:
$$ Q_h^{\pi^t}(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ (P_hV_{h+1}^{\pi^t})(s,a) $$
Then improve the policy greedily:
$$ \pi_h^{t+1}(s)= \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}} Q_h^{\pi^t}(s,a), \qquad \forall s,h $$
Here the policy is a global policy map. It is not only choosing one action for one state. It updates the decision rule for all states.
This is important because planning is not a local one-step trick. The policy improvement step changes the global behavior of the agent.
With exact policy evaluation and exact greedy improvement, finite-horizon policy iteration can be understood as propagating improved decisions backward through time.
The intuition is simple.
At the first iteration, the policy can make the correct decision near the terminal state. At the next iteration, this improved decision is propagated one step earlier. Repeating this process spreads the improved decisions backward through time.
After enough iterations, the improvement has propagated through the whole horizon.
So policy iteration can be understood as:
$$ \text{policy evaluation}\rightarrow\text{policy improvement}\rightarrow\text{policy evaluation}\rightarrow\cdots $$
3. What if the Horizon Goes to Infinity? The previous discussion assumes a finite horizon. But many RL problems are naturally infinite-horizon problems.
If we simply sum all future rewards,
$$ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}r_t $$
the return may become unbounded.
To avoid this, we introduce a discount factor:
$$ \gamma\in(0,1) $$
An infinite-horizon discounted MDP can be written as
$$ \text{MDP}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,P,\gamma) $$
The value function becomes
$$ V^\pi(s)= E_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r_t \mid s_0=s \right] $$
The discount factor has two meanings.
First, it makes the infinite sum finite, as we have discussed in note.
Second, it makes rewards in the far future less important.
To see the effective horizon, consider the discounted tail after step $h$: Assume rewards are bounded,then $$ \sum_{t=h}^{\infty}\gamma^t= \gamma^h \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k= \frac{\gamma^h}{1-\gamma} $$
If we want this tail to be smaller than $\epsilon$, we need
$$ \frac{\gamma^h}{1-\gamma}\leq \epsilon $$
Taking log function gives
$$ h\log\gamma \leq \log((1-\gamma)\epsilon) $$
Since $\log\gamma<0$, we get
$$ h \geq \frac{\log(1/((1-\gamma)\epsilon))}{-\log\gamma} $$
When $\gamma$ is close to 1, we use the approximation
$$ -\log\gamma\approx 1-\gamma $$
Therefore,
$$ h \gtrsim \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \log \left( \frac{1}{(1-\gamma)\epsilon} \right)= \tilde{\mathcal{O}} \left( \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \right) $$
This tells us that the effective horizon of a discounted MDP is roughly
$$ \frac{1}{1-\gamma} $$
So even though the problem is infinite-horizon, discounting makes it behave like a long but finite-horizon problem.
4. Bellman Optimality in the Infinite-Horizon Case In the infinite-horizon discounted setting, the Bellman optimality equation becomes time-independent.
The optimal value satisfies
$$ V^\star(s)= \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V^\star(s’) \right] \right) $$
The optimal Q-function satisfies
$$ Q^\star(s,a)= r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ \max_{a’}Q^\star(s’,a’) \right] $$
Once $Q^\star$ is known, the optimal policy is simply
$$ \pi^\star(s)= \arg\max_a Q^\star(s,a) $$
This is the infinite-horizon version of the same idea:
value tells us which action is good, and the policy follows the action with the best value.
5. Summary This section connects value computation to policy optimization.
The core logic is:
$$ \text{Bellman equation}\rightarrow\text{value function}\rightarrow\text{policy improvement} $$
For finite-horizon problems, we can prove optimality by backward induction.
For known environments, we can solve the problem by planning, mainly through value iteration or policy iteration.
For infinite-horizon problems, discounting makes the return finite and introduces an effective horizon:
$$ H_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx \frac{1}{1-\gamma} $$
So the big picture is:
$$ \text{RL is not only about estimating value. It is about using value to act better.} $$
6. Application Here we briefly introduce a method that leverages the idea of learning a transition model to improve policy learning.
In previous sections, planning assumes that the transition model is known. However, in real RL scenarios, the true transition model is usually unknown. Dreamer addresses this problem by learning a latent world model from interaction data [4]. In a simplified view, Dreamer learns a latent dynamics model: $$ z_{t+1}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid z_t,a_t) $$
where $z_t$ is a compact latent state learned from observations.
Once this model is learned, Dreamer can imagine future trajectories in latent space:
$$ z_t,a_t,\hat{r_t},z_{t+1},a_{t+1},\hat{r}_{t+1},\dots $$
Then the actor and critic are trained on these imagined futures. In this sense, Dreamer connects back to the planning idea discussed above: when the true transition model is unavailable, it learns a transition model and uses the imagined futures from this model to train the policy and value function.
The following figure shows the pipeline of the classic Dreamer algorithm. Later variants have extended this framework, but the core idea remains similar [4, 5, 6].
Figure: Classic Dreamer pipeline. Adapted from Hafner et al., 2020 [4]. References [1] Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd edition, MIT Press, 2018.
Available online: http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html
[2] Richard Bellman. Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press, 1957.
[3] Martin L. Puterman. Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming. Wiley, 1994.
[4] Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Jimmy Ba, and Mohammad Norouzi. Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination. ICLR, 2020.
[5] Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Mohammad Norouzi, and Jimmy Ba. Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models. ICLR, 2021.
[6] Danijar Hafner, Jurgis Pasukonis, Jimmy Ba, and Timothy Lillicrap. Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models. arXiv, 2023.

content:
How does an agent learn a behavior when no one can tell it the correct action at every state? This question is especially important in on-policy RL, where we do not first obtain an action-value function that reliably covers the entire state–action space and then derive the “optimal” action from it. Instead, we specify what counts as a good outcome, let the current policy interact with the environment, and use the resulting experience to make better behavior more likely.
The Policy Changes Its Own Data A different policy does not merely make different decisions; it also generates different experience. In supervised learning, updating a model changes its predictions while leaving the training data unchanged. In reinforcement learning, however, the policy helps generate its own data. Its actions affect the next states, those states affect the decisions that follow, and together they determine the trajectories from which the policy learns.
At iteration (k), the process can be written schematically as
$$ \pi^{(k)} \longrightarrow \mathcal{D}^{(k)} \sim p(\tau \mid \pi^{(k)}) \longrightarrow \pi^{(k+1)}. $$
The dataset ($\mathcal{D}_k$) is not an independent sample of everything the agent might experience. It reflects the states visited and actions chosen by ($\pi_k$). Once the policy is updated, ($\pi _ {k+1}$) may generate a different trajectory distribution—and therefore a different learning problem.
why previous collected data is not eligible? Value estimation propagates the consequences of a trajectory backward: rewards observed later are discounted when they are assigned to earlier states and actions. Because our experience does not cover the entire state–action space, we cannot directly know the optimal action at every state. We can only compare actions using the data we have collected.
Ideally, the data used to estimate a policy’s value would all come from that same fixed policy—not necessarily the optimal policy, but the policy we are evaluating. When both the environment and the policy are fixed, the induced trajectory distribution is fixed, and the return has a stable interpretation. Using the notation in TRPO [3], the state–action value is
$$ Q^\pi(s_t,a_t)= \mathbb{E} _ {s _ {t+1},a_{t+1},\ldots\sim\pi} \left[ \sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty} \gamma^\ell r_{t+\ell} \right]. $$
The superscript ($\pi$) matters: after taking ($a_t$), the subsequent actions contributing to this return are still generated by ($\pi$).
But the policy being trained is not fixed. As it learns and updates, its future actions change, along with the states it visits and the outcomes that follow an earlier decision. The recorded return of an old trajectory does not itself change, but it estimates ($Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}}$), not ($Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{current}}}$). Consequently, an action ranking inferred from old data may no longer be trustworthy for the current policy, especially when we retain trajectories collected during much earlier stages of training.
Consider a robot learning to grasp a cup at different stages of training. Under the current policy, action ($a_1$) may be better than ($a_2$) because it moves the gripper into a state from which the robot can complete a stable grasp. Under an early policy, however, the same ($a_1$) may be followed by poor corrective actions and end with the cup being knocked over. Those early trajectories therefore assign ($a_1$) a low return. If we treat that return as an estimate of its value under the current policy, ($a_1$) may be rejected even though it has now become the better action. The environment has not changed; the policy that acts after ($a_1$) has.
An action can receive a poor return under an early policy because of what that policy does next, even when the same action becomes useful under the current policy. This is why on-policy methods refresh their experience—and why, when a batch is reused, the next question is how far the policy can move before that batch stops being a reliable basis for improvement.
What Makes One Policy Better Than Another? Policy improvement turns the idea of “better behavior” into a precise comparison. Starting from a current policy ($\pi$), we want to construct another policy ($\pi’$) with a higher expected return:
$$ J(\pi’) > J(\pi). $$
The inequality tells us how to recognize a better policy, but not how to identify one using data generated by a different policy (like the current policy). To reason about that change in advance, we need a reference provided by the policy we already understand.
For the current policy ($\pi$), ($V^\pi(s)$) describes the expected return from state ($s$), while ($Q^\pi(s,a)$) describes the expected return after taking ($a$) and then continuing with ($\pi$). Their difference is the advantage:
$$ A^\pi(s,a)= Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s). $$
A positive advantage does not mean that an action is universally good. It means that taking the action once and then following ($\pi$) is better than the behavior that ($\pi$) produces on average from the same state. In a fully known tabular problem, knowing these comparisons everywhere would allow us to improve the policy directly.
More generally, the exact relationship between two policies is given by the performance-difference lemma [1]:
$$ J(\pi’)-J(\pi)= \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \mathbb{E}_{s\sim d _ {\pi’},a\sim\pi’(\cdot\mid s)} \left[ A^\pi(s,a) \right], $$
where ($d_{\pi’}$) is the normalized discounted state-visitation distribution induced by ($\pi’$). The exact identity is not yet usable with the data we have. Its state distribution $d _ {\pi’}$ describes the states that the candidate policy will visit, but those states are unavailable until we actually run $\pi’$. We therefore make the central local approximation: keep the current policy’s advantage function, but evaluate the candidate policy at states visited by the current policy. Replacing $d _ {\pi’}$ with $d _ \pi$ gives the surrogate
$$ L _ \pi(\pi’)= J(\pi)+ \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \mathbb{E} _ {s\sim d _ \pi,,a\sim\pi’(\cdot\mid s)} \bigl[ A^\pi(s,a) \bigr]. $$
This removes the need to sample states from $\pi’$, but it is not yet a finite-batch estimator: the actions in the batch were sampled from $\pi$, and $A^\pi$ is still unknown. The next step is to express both quantities using the data collected under the current policy.
The actions in the batch were also sampled from ($\pi$), but their distribution can be reweighted using a probability ratio:
$$ \mathbb{E} _ {s\sim d_\pi,a\sim\pi} \left[ \frac{\pi’(a\mid s)} {\pi(a\mid s)} A^\pi(s,a) \right]. $$
Given a batch $$ \mathcal{D} _ \pi= {(s_t,a_t,\widehat{A} _ t)} _ {t=1}^{N}. $$
where $\widehat{A}$ is the estimate advantage, the part of the surrogate relevant for optimization can therefore be estimated as
$$ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{\pi’(a _ t\mid s_t)} {\pi(a_t\mid s_t)} \widehat{A} _ t. $$
This estimator is computable from current-policy data. The probability ratio adjusts how the candidate policy weights the sampled actions, but it does not change the sampled states from ($d_\pi$) into states from ($d_{\pi’}$). The surrogate is therefore reliable near the current policy, where the two state distributions remain similar, but can become misleading after a large update. The next question is how to optimize this objective without moving the policy beyond the region in which the approximation can be trusted.
Which Way Should the Policy Move? In tabular policy improvement, this question can be answered one state at a time. If $Q^\pi(s,a)$ is known for every action, we can inspect the corresponding row of the policy table and choose $a^*(s)=\arg\max_a Q^\pi(s,a)$.
For a stochastic policy, the same idea means assigning more probability to actions with positive advantage and less to actions with negative advantage. Because every state has its own row in the table, changing the decision at one state does not have to change the decisions at other states.
A neural policy does not have this independence. The same parameter vector $\theta$ determines the action distribution $\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$ at every state. Changing $\theta$ to favor an action at one state may also change the policy’s behavior at many other states. We therefore need a single direction in parameter space that combines the improvement signals from all samples in the batch.
Let the current policy be $\pi_{\theta_k}$, and let $\pi_\theta$ represent a candidate policy. The sample-based objective from the previous section becomes
$$ \widehat{L} _ k(\theta)= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_k}(a_t\mid s_t)} \widehat{A} _ t. $$
At the beginning of the update, $\theta=\theta_k$, so the candidate and the data-generating policy are identical. Because the policy is differentiable, we can ask which small change in $\theta$ would increase this objective most quickly. Evaluating its gradient at the current parameters gives
$$ \widehat{g} _ k= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \widehat{A} _ t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t) \quad \text{at }\theta=\theta_k. $$
At this point, the probability ratio equals one, and its derivative becomes the gradient of the log probability. Each sample then contributes a simple signal: a positive $\widehat{A}_t$ pushes toward increasing the probability of the sampled action, while a negative $\widehat{A}_t$ pushes in the opposite direction. For a detailed derivation of why this likelihood-ratio form yields a gradient that can be estimated from experience, see Sutton et al [2].
A basic gradient-ascent step produces the candidate policy:
$$ \theta _ {k+1}= \theta_k+\alpha\widehat{g} _ k, \qquad \pi’= \pi _ {\theta_{k+1}}. $$
At the current policy, the surrogate and the true performance objective agree to first order, so the gradient gives a locally valid direction. But the gradient only describes the objective at the point where the data and policy still match. Once the optimizer takes a finite step, that match begins to break, and the objective becomes a less reliable guide to actual policy improvement.
When a Good Direction Becomes a Bad Update The distinction between a direction and an update matters. A gradient is a first-order statement about what happens near the current parameters. Like a first-order Taylor approximation, it replaces the objective’s curved surface with a tangent plane around $\theta_k$:
$$ J(\theta_k+\Delta\theta)= J(\theta_k)+ \nabla_\theta J(\theta_k)^\top\Delta\theta+ \mathcal{O}(\lVert\Delta\theta\rVert^2). $$
Close to $\theta_k$, the tangent plane follows the actual objective well. Farther away, the curvature hidden in the higher-order terms becomes increasingly important. Moving along the gradient makes the first-order term positive, so a sufficiently small step provides a useful prediction of improvement. A practical optimizer, however, takes a finite step and often takes several of them on the same batch. As the policy moves farther from $\pi_{\theta_k}$, the terms ignored by this local approximation become harder to dismiss.
The gradient defines a local direction at the current policy. A small step follows the true objective closely, while a large step may continue to look beneficial under the first-order approximation even after the actual return has decreased. In policy optimization, the local approximation is also tied to the policy that generated the data.
A good direction becomes a bad update when the candidate policy moves far enough that the old batch no longer represents its behavior. Large or repeated steps may continue to increase $\widehat{L}_k(\theta)$ on the same samples, while the state distribution shifts and repeated use of noisy $\widehat{A}_t$ magnifies estimation error. The optimizer may still be improving the empirical objective even after that objective has stopped tracking the true return.
The issue is therefore not whether the gradient was correct at $\theta_k$, but how far the policy can move before its local approximation and supporting data become unreliable.
How far we can trust the update A natural answer is to limit the parameter change $\lVert\theta-\theta_k\rVert$. But parameter distance is a poor measure of behavioral change. The same parameter step can barely affect the policy in some states while sharply changing its action probabilities in others. What matters is not how far the parameters move, but how differently the new policy behaves.
For a stochastic policy, this change can be measured by the KL divergence between its old and new action distributions:
$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}} \left( \pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s) ,\Vert, \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s) \right). $$
A small KL divergence means that, at state $s$, the candidate policy still assigns similar probabilities to actions as the policy that generated the data. TRPO [3] turns this idea into an explicit constraint:
$$ \max_\theta \widehat{L} _ k(\theta) \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad \mathbb{E} _ {s\sim d_{\pi_{\theta_k}}} \left[ D_{\mathrm{KL}} \left( \pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s) ,\Vert, \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s) \right) \right] \leq \delta. $$
The objective asks the policy to improve according to the current batch; the constraint limits how much its behavior may change while doing so. The reasoning behind this constraint can be summarized as
$$ \text{penalty for policy change}. $$
In the theoretical argument, this penalty depends on the largest KL divergence across states. Practical TRPO instead constrains the average KL divergence over states visited by the old policy, because a worst-case change cannot be measured reliably from a finite batch. This replacement is itself an approximation.
The trust region therefore does not make old data perfectly valid for the new policy. It limits how far the optimizer is allowed to extrapolate from that data. TRPO provides a principled way to impose this limit, but doing so requires a constrained, second-order optimization procedure and a line search. PPO keeps the same concern while asking whether proximity can be encouraged through a simpler modification of the objective itself.
PPO as a Design Decision PPO is not an inevitable consequence of policy improvement. It is one practical answer to the problem left by TRPO: how can we reuse an on-policy batch for several first-order updates without allowing the policy to move too far from the behavior that generated it?
The probability ratio introduced earlier provides a direct way to observe this movement:
$$ r_t(\theta)= \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)} {\pi_{\theta_k}(a_t\mid s_t)}. $$
At the beginning of optimization, $\theta=\theta_k$ and every ratio is one. If $\widehat{A}_t>0$, increasing $r_t(\theta)$ makes the sampled action more likely. If $\widehat{A}_t<0$, decreasing the ratio makes it less likely. The unclipped objective continues to reward these changes regardless of how far the ratio has already moved.
PPO [4] changes the shape of this objective:
$$ \widehat{L}^{\mathrm{CLIP}}_k(\theta)= \frac{1}{N} \sum _ {t=1}^{N} \min \left( r _ t(\theta)\widehat{A} _ t,, \operatorname{clip} \left( r _ t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon \right) \widehat{A} _ t \right). $$
For a positive advantage, the objective stops providing additional benefit once the action probability has increased beyond $1+\epsilon$. For a negative advantage, the benefit stops once the probability has decreased below $1-\epsilon$. The minimum selects the more conservative contribution, making the clipped term a pessimistic version of the original sample objective—not a lower bound on the policy’s true return.
This distinction matters: clipping does not force every ratio to remain inside $[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]$. It only removes the incentive from a particular sample to move farther in the direction suggested by its advantage. Other samples controlled by the same network can still push that ratio outside the interval.
Clipping is also inactive at the start of each iteration because all ratios initially equal one. Its role appears after several minibatch updates, when the optimized policy begins to depart from $\pi_{\theta_k}$. This is what allows PPO to perform multiple optimization epochs on one batch while gradually reducing the benefit of increasingly aggressive changes.
What clipping does not do is refresh the states in the batch or recompute their advantages under the new policy. It controls changes in the probabilities of sampled actions at sampled states; it does not directly control the unseen trajectory distribution that those changes may produce.
PPO therefore replaces TRPO’s explicit distribution-level constraint with a per-sample modification of the objective. The trade-off is deliberate: simpler first-order optimization and greater data reuse in exchange for a weaker notion of proximity and no guarantee that the resulting update remains inside a true trust region. Seen this way, PPO is not the final form of policy optimization, but one choice about where and how to be conservative.
Think Beyond PPO Thinking beyond PPO does not begin by asking how to invent another clipping function. It begins by asking which approximation in the current update no longer matches the problem.
A policy-gradient update can be viewed schematically as
$$ \widehat{g} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum _ {t=1}^{N} c _ t(\theta)\widehat{A} _ t \nabla _ \theta \log\pi _ \theta(a _ t\mid s _ t). $$
Here, $\widehat{A} _ t$ determines what behavior should be reinforced, while $c _ t(\theta)$ describes how the evidence is corrected and how strongly it may change the policy. Recent algorithms can appear similar to PPO while changing either of these choices.
Change how improvement is estimated. GRPO [5] removes the learned value function and compares several trajectories generated from the same initial condition:
$$ \widehat{A} _ i= \frac{ R _ i-\frac{1}{G}\sum _ {j=1}^{G}R _ j }{ \operatorname{std}(R _ 1,\ldots,R _ G) }. $$
In language-model training, these trajectories are responses generated for the same prompt. A response with above-average reward receives a positive advantage, while one with below-average reward receives a negative advantage.
GRPO otherwise retains the PPO-style probability ratio and clipping objective. Its main decision is therefore not to change how far the policy may move, but to change the reference used to decide which trajectories are better. This removes the critic, but it also makes the learning signal depend on the other trajectories sampled in the same group.
Change the unit at which policy mismatch is measured. In an autoregressive policy, each token is an action, its preceding prefix is the state, and the complete response is a trajectory. GRPO applies PPO-style clipping to the probability ratio of each individual token. GSPO [6] instead defines one length-normalized ratio for the complete response:
$$ s _ i(\theta)= \bigg( \frac{ \pi _ \theta(y _ i\mid x) }{ \pi _ {\theta _ k}(y _ i\mid x) } \bigg)^{\frac{1}{|y _ i|}}. $$
This ratio is the geometric mean of the probability changes along the response. GSPO applies clipping and optimization at this sequence level rather than deciding separately whether each token has moved too far.
The change is subtle but important. If reward evaluates the complete trajectory, token-level clipping may treat the decisions within that trajectory as unrelated updates. Sequence-level clipping instead asks whether the behavior that produced the complete outcome has collectively moved away from the policy that generated the data.
The length normalization keeps the ratio numerically manageable, but it also means that $s _ i(\theta)$ is not the exact importance ratio between the two trajectory distributions. GSPO therefore does not eliminate approximation. It chooses a different one: greater alignment between the reward and update granularity in exchange for an inexact distribution correction.
GRPO and GSPO illustrate two distinct places where a new policy objective can intervene. GRPO changes the improvement signal while largely preserving PPO’s update mechanism. GSPO retains the group-relative signal but changes what counts as a policy change.
Future progress may therefore come not from a universally better clipping rule, but from objectives that make their assumptions about data, credit, and policy movement explicit. The central question remains the one that began this post: how can an agent learn better behavior from experience without pushing its policy a step too far?

[2] Richard S. Sutton, David McAllester, Satinder Singh, and Yishay Mansour. Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation. NeurIPS, 1999.
[3] John Schulman, Sergey Levine, Pieter Abbeel, Michael Jordan, and Philipp Moritz. Trust Region Policy Optimization. ICML, 2015.
[4] John Schulman, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, and Oleg Klimov. Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. arXiv, 2017.
[5] Zhihong Shao, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, Runxin Xu, Junxian Song, Mingchuan Zhang, Y.K. Li, Y. Wu, and Daya Guo. DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. arXiv, 2024.
[6] Group Sequence Policy Optimization. arXiv, 2025.
summary: How does an agent learn a behavior when no one can tell it the correct action at every state? This question is especially important in on-policy RL, where we do not first obtain an action-value function that reliably covers the entire state–action space and then derive the “optimal” action from it. Instead, we specify what counts as a good outcome, let the current policy interact with the environment, and use the resulting experience to make better behavior more likely.

title: Hello World

content:
1. What is Reinforcement Learning? Reinforcement Learning (RL), at its core, is a method of learning. Learning based on wikipedia, is the process of acquiring new understanding and knowledge. To simplify it: when you see something, you know something more than that.
Some classic ways of learning can be shown as examples.
In supervised learning, we learn from supervised examples:
$$ \text{input} \rightarrow \text{target} $$
The model sees an input and is taught what the correct corresponding target should be. If we later see a different input with the same label, we learn to associate it with the same target.
In unsupervised learning, we are not given explicit labels. Instead, the model tries to discover hidden structures, patterns, or relationships within the data by itself. Reinforcement Learning is different. In RL, an agent learns by interacting with an environment. It takes actions, observes the consequences, receives rewards, which are not necessarily just numbers, and gradually reinforces its behavior toward directions that may lead to higher long-term return.
So RL is not only about one-step causal reasoning. It is about training a policy and developing an understanding of value. A policy answers:
$$ \text{What should I do?} $$
A value function answers:
$$ \text{How good is this situation, if I keep behaving like this?} $$
2. Markov Assumption and Policy Forms When studying RL, we usually begin with an important assumption: the environment satisfies the Markov property.
$$ P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, \dots)= P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t) $$
This means that, given the current state and action, the next state no longer depends on the entire past history.
In other words, the current state is assumed to contain all the information needed for predicting the future.
Under this assumption, we can define two broad forms of policies.
A Markov policy only depends on the current state:
$$ \pi_\theta(a \mid s): \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \Delta(\mathcal{A}) $$
A more general history-dependent policy may depend on the full trajectory so far:
$$ \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_{1:t}, a_{1:t-1}) $$
In principle, a general policy has more information. It can look at the whole past. But in a Markov environment, the current state already summarizes the useful part of the past.
The goal of both policies is the same: maximize the expected return from the initial state.
$$ \max_\pi V^\pi(s_1) $$
3. Why is a Markov Policy Enough? A beautiful result in RL says that, in a Markov environment, we do not lose optimality by restricting ourselves to Markov policies.
More formally, for any history-dependent policy $\pi$, there exists a Markov policy $\mu$ such that
$$ V^{\pi}(s_1) \leq V^\mu(s_1) $$
The intuition is simple.
If the state really contains all information needed for future prediction, then the agent does not need to remember the entire past. At each state, it only needs to choose an action that leads to the best possible future.
So the optimal decision can be made from the current state alone.
This is one of the reasons why Markov Decision Processes are so central in RL. They give us a clean mathematical world where memory can be replaced by state [3].
4. How Do We Know Whether a Policy is Good? In RL, the objective is special: what we optimize is also how we measure success. The goal itself becomes the metric — accumulated reward.
If a policy achieves a higher return, we call it better.
In a finite-horizon setting, the value function is defined as
$$ V_h^\pi(s)= E_{\pi} \left[ \sum_{\tau=h}^{H} r(s_{\tau}, a_{\tau}) \mid s_h = s \right] $$
It means: starting from state $s$ at time $h$, if we follow policy $\pi$, what total reward do we expect to collect until the end?
The action-value function, or Q-function, also conditions on the first action:
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= E_\pi \left[ \sum_{h’=h}^{H} r(s_{h’}, a_{h’}) \mid s_h = s, a_h = a \right] $$
So $V^\pi$ tells us how good a state is, while $Q^\pi$ tells us how good a state-action pair is.
This small difference is extremely important. Once we know $Q^\pi(s,a)$, action selection becomes easier: we can compare actions directly.
5. Monte Carlo Estimation of Value One natural way to estimate value is very direct: start from a state, roll out the policy many times, and average the returns.
This is the Monte Carlo idea [1].
$$ V^\pi(s) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( \sum_{h=1}^{H} r(s_h, a_h) \right)_i $$
Here, $N$ is the number of sampled episodes, and $H$ is the horizon length.
Monte Carlo estimation is conceptually clean. If we sample enough trajectories, the average return becomes a good estimate of the true value.
But the problem is variance.
To see this, consider a simplified infinite-horizon discounted return:
$$ G = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_t $$
Assume the rewards are independent and identically distributed:
$$ r_t \sim \mathcal{D}, \qquad E[r_t] = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(r_t) = \sigma^2 $$
Then the variance of the return is
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(G) &= \mathrm{Var} \left( \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_t \right) &= \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{2t} \mathrm{Var}(r_t) &= \sigma^2 \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} (\gamma^2)^t &= \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\gamma^2} \end{aligned} $$
When $\gamma$ approaches 1, the horizon becomes effectively long. Since
$$ 1-\gamma^2= (1-\gamma)(1+\gamma) \approx 2(1-\gamma) $$
we get
$$ \mathrm{Var}(G) \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{2(1-\gamma)} $$
This shows why Monte Carlo methods can be noisy in long-horizon problems. The longer the effective horizon, the more future randomness is accumulated into the return estimate.
Also, in real scenarios, rewards are rarely i.i.d. The reward at one step is often related to what happened before and what will happen next, so the randomness does not simply average out. This makes estimating return even more unstable.
6. Bellman Equation: Computing Value Recursively The Bellman equation gives another way to compute value recursively, and is the core idea behind dynamic programming in sequential decision problems [2].
Instead of waiting until the end of the episode, it breaks the return into two parts:
the immediate reward; the value of the next state. For a fixed policy $\pi$, the expectation Bellman equation is
$$ V_h^\pi(s)= \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) Q_h^\pi(s,a) $$
and
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= r_h(s,a) + E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] $$
This is the central recursive idea in RL.
A value is not estimated only by rolling out to the end. It can also be estimated by looking one step ahead and bootstrapping from another value estimate.
In the infinite-horizon discounted case, a typical one-step TD target is
$$ Q(s_t,a_t)= r_t + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) $$
Compared with Monte Carlo, this target depends only on the immediate reward and the estimated value of the next state-action pair.
Its randomness mainly comes from two sources:
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var} \left( r_t + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) \right) &= \mathrm{Var}(r_t) + \gamma^2 \mathrm{Var}_{s’ \sim P} \left( Q(s’,a’) \right) \end{aligned} $$
This is often much lower variance than summing rewards over a long trajectory.
But this lower variance is not free.
7. What Does Bellman Bootstrapping Sacrifice? Monte Carlo estimation is unbiased in the sense that, if we sample complete trajectories, the expected return equals the true value:
$$ E[G_t] = V^\pi(s_t) $$
Bellman-style methods use bootstrapping. The target depends on the current estimate of the value function.
For example, if we use a parameterized Q-function $Q_\theta$, then the target itself contains $Q_\theta$:
$$ r_t + \gamma Q_\theta(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) $$
This introduces bias, especially early in training when $Q_\theta$ is inaccurate.
So there is a classic trade-off:
$$ \text{Monte Carlo: low bias, high variance} $$
$$ \text{Bellman / TD: higher bias during learning, lower variance} $$
A large part of RL algorithm design can be understood as navigating this trade-off.
8. Convergence of the Bellman Equation Since Bellman methods rely on their own current estimates, a natural question appears:
Why should this process converge?
To answer this, we need the idea of a fixed point.
For optimal control, the Bellman optimality equation is
$$ V_h(s)= \max_a Q_h(s,a) $$
with
$$ Q_h(s,a)= r_h(s,a) + \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V*{h+1}(s’) \right] $$
The expectation Bellman equation evaluates a fixed policy. The optimality Bellman equation searches for the best policy.
This reflects a deep duality in RL:
policy evaluation asks: how good is this policy? policy optimization asks: how good can we possibly be? To study convergence, define the Bellman optimality operator $\mathcal{T}$:
$$ (\mathcal{T}V)(s)= \max_a \left( r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) V(s’) \right) $$
Then solving the Bellman equation is equivalent to finding a fixed point:
$$ V = \mathcal{T}V $$
8.1 Banach Fixed Point Theorem The mathematical tool behind this convergence story is the Banach Fixed Point Theorem [4].
Let $(X,d)$ be a complete metric space. Suppose $\mathcal{T}: X \rightarrow X$ is a contraction mapping, meaning that for some $0 \leq \gamma < 1$,
$$ d(\mathcal{T}u, \mathcal{T}v) \leq \gamma d(u,v), \qquad \forall u,v \in X $$
Then three things hold.
First, $\mathcal{T}$ has a unique fixed point $V^*$:
$$ \mathcal{T}V^* = V^* $$
Second, starting from any initial guess $V_0$, the sequence
$$ V_{k+1} = \mathcal{T}V_k $$
converges to $V^*$.
Third, the error decreases geometrically. For example, an a priori bound is
$$ d(V_k, V^*) \leq \frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma} d(V_1,V_0) $$
and an a posteriori bound is
$$ d(V_k,V^*) \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} d(V_k,V_{k-1}) $$
This theorem gives the formal backbone of value iteration [1, 3].
8.2 Why is the Bellman Operator a Contraction? We can prove that the Bellman optimality operator shrinks the distance between any two value functions.
Using the infinity norm,
$$ \lVert V-U \rVert_\infty= \max_s |V(s)-U(s)| $$
we have
$$ \begin{aligned} \left| {T}V - {T}U \right|_\infty &= \max_s \left| ({T}V)(s)- ({T}U)(s) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &= \max_s \left| \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V(s’) \right] \right)- \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ U(s’) \right] \right) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &\leq \max_s \max_a \left| \gamma \operatorname{E}_{s’ \sim P(\cdot \mid s,a)} \left[ V(s’) - U(s’) \right] \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &= \gamma \max_s \max_a \left| \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) \left( V(s’) - U(s’) \right) \right| \end{aligned} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} &\leq \gamma \max_s \max_a \sum_{s’} P(s’ \mid s,a) \left| V(s’) - U(s’) \right| \ &\leq \gamma \left| V-U \right|_\infty . \end{aligned} $$ Because $\gamma < 1$, the Bellman operator is a contraction mapping.
Therefore, by the Banach Fixed Point Theorem, value iteration converges to the unique fixed point $V^*$.
This is one of the most elegant results in RL: a simple recursive update can be guaranteed to converge, not because of magic, but because each Bellman update pulls value estimates closer together.
References [1] Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. 2nd edition, MIT Press, 2018.
*Available online: http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html
[2] Richard Bellman. Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press, 1957.
[3] Martin L. Puterman. Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming. Wiley, 1994.
[4] Stefan Banach. “Sur les opérations dans les ensembles abstraits et leur application aux équations intégrales.” Fundamenta Mathematicae, 3:133–181, 1922.

Preface In the previous note, we introduced the basic idea of Reinforcement Learning and discussed how the Bellman equation can be used to compute the value function.
Intuitively, the value function tells us how much future return we can expect from a state, or from taking a particular action in that state.
In this section, we go one step further.
If value tells us how good something is, then a natural question is:
$$ \text{How can we use value to improve the policy?} $$
In other words, we now move from policy evaluation to policy optimization.
1. Bellman Optimality Equation Leads to the Optimal Policy Earlier, we used the Bellman equation to compute value under a fixed policy.
Now we want to use the Bellman optimality equation as a training goal. But before doing that, we should first ask:
$$ \text{If we solve the Bellman optimality equation, can it really give us the optimal policy?} $$
For a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process, we want to prove that
$$ V_h^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_h^\pi(s), \qquad \forall h,s $$
The proof can be understood by backward induction.
Assume that at time $h+1$, the optimal value is already correct:
$$ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_{h+1}^\pi(s), \qquad \forall s $$
We want to show that this also holds at time $h$.
At the terminal step, the agent receives no future reward after the horizon, so
$$ V_{H+1}^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_{H+1}^\pi(s)=0 $$
This gives the base case.
Now consider the action-value function. For any state-action pair $(s,a)$,
$$ Q_h^\pi(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] $$
Taking the maximum over policies gives
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_\pi \left( r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] \right) &= r_h(s,a)+ \max_\pi E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\pi(s’) \right] \end{aligned} $$
By the induction assumption, the optimal continuation value at time $h+1$ satisfies
$$ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s’)= \max_\pi V_{h+1}^\pi(s’), \qquad \forall s' $$
Since a policy can choose actions based on the state it reaches, the optimal continuation policy can be used for every possible next state $s’$. Therefore,
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= r_h(s,a)+ E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^{\pi^\star}(s’) \right] &= Q_h^{\pi^\star}(s,a) \end{aligned} $$
Now we convert from $Q$ to $V$.
For a stochastic policy, $V_h^\pi(s)$ is an expectation over actions. But the optimal policy can put all probability mass on the best action. Therefore,
$$ \begin{aligned} \max_\pi V_h^\pi(s) &= \max_\pi \sum_a \pi(a\mid s)Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_a \max_\pi Q_h^\pi(s,a) &= \max_a Q_h^{\pi^\star}(s,a) &= V_h^{\pi^\star}(s) \end{aligned} $$
So by backward induction,
$$ V_h^{\pi^\star}(s)=\max_\pi V_h^\pi(s), \qquad \forall h,s $$
The whole point is simple:
If the future value is already optimal, then choosing the action that leads to the best future gives the optimal value now.
2. Solving the Problem by Planning Now we know that if the optimal value function is known, then the optimal policy can be recovered by choosing the action with the highest value.
This gives us a direct solution method: planning.
In the planning setting, we assume the environment model is known:
$$ \text{Env}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,P) $$
That means we know both the reward function $r$ and the transition probability $P$.
The goal is then:
$$ \text{given } r \text{ and } P,\quad \text{compute } \pi^\star $$
This is often called the simulation setting or model-based planning setting.
There are two classical ways to do this.
2.1 Value Iteration Value iteration directly applies the Bellman optimality equation.
For a finite-horizon MDP, initialize
$$ V_{H+1}^\star(s)=0 $$
Then for
$$ h=H,H-1,\dots,0 $$
we compute
$$ Q_h^\star(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ (P_hV_{h+1}^\star)(s,a), \qquad \forall s,a $$
where
$$ (P_hV_{h+1}^\star)(s,a)= E_{s’\sim P_h(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V_{h+1}^\star(s’) \right] $$
Then update
$$ V_h^\star(s)=\max_a Q_h^\star(s,a) $$
After computing the optimal value, the optimal policy is obtained by
$$ \pi_h^\star(s)= \arg\max_a Q_h^\star(s,a) $$
Intuitively, value iteration works backward in time:
$$ \text{future value}\rightarrow\text{current value}\rightarrow\text{current action} $$
It builds a global value map first, and then uses this value map to guide the actor.
2.2 Policy Iteration Policy iteration takes another view.
Instead of directly updating the value toward the optimal Bellman equation, it alternates between two steps:
evaluate the current policy; improve the policy using the current value. Initialize an arbitrary policy:
$$ \pi^0 $$
At iteration $t$, first do policy evaluation:
$$ Q_h^{\pi^t}(s,a)= r_h(s,a)+ (P_hV_{h+1}^{\pi^t})(s,a) $$
Then improve the policy greedily:
$$ \pi_h^{t+1}(s)= \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}} Q_h^{\pi^t}(s,a), \qquad \forall s,h $$
Here the policy is a global policy map. It is not only choosing one action for one state. It updates the decision rule for all states.
This is important because planning is not a local one-step trick. The policy improvement step changes the global behavior of the agent.
With exact policy evaluation and exact greedy improvement, finite-horizon policy iteration can be understood as propagating improved decisions backward through time.
The intuition is simple.
At the first iteration, the policy can make the correct decision near the terminal state. At the next iteration, this improved decision is propagated one step earlier. Repeating this process spreads the improved decisions backward through time.
After enough iterations, the improvement has propagated through the whole horizon.
So policy iteration can be understood as:
$$ \text{policy evaluation}\rightarrow\text{policy improvement}\rightarrow\text{policy evaluation}\rightarrow\cdots $$
3. What if the Horizon Goes to Infinity? The previous discussion assumes a finite horizon. But many RL problems are naturally infinite-horizon problems.
If we simply sum all future rewards,
$$ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}r_t $$
the return may become unbounded.
To avoid this, we introduce a discount factor:
$$ \gamma\in(0,1) $$
An infinite-horizon discounted MDP can be written as
$$ \text{MDP}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,P,\gamma) $$
The value function becomes
$$ V^\pi(s)= E_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r_t \mid s_0=s \right] $$
The discount factor has two meanings.
First, it makes the infinite sum finite, as we have discussed in note.
Second, it makes rewards in the far future less important.
To see the effective horizon, consider the discounted tail after step $h$: Assume rewards are bounded,then $$ \sum_{t=h}^{\infty}\gamma^t= \gamma^h \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k= \frac{\gamma^h}{1-\gamma} $$
If we want this tail to be smaller than $\epsilon$, we need
$$ \frac{\gamma^h}{1-\gamma}\leq \epsilon $$
Taking log function gives
$$ h\log\gamma \leq \log((1-\gamma)\epsilon) $$
Since $\log\gamma<0$, we get
$$ h \geq \frac{\log(1/((1-\gamma)\epsilon))}{-\log\gamma} $$
When $\gamma$ is close to 1, we use the approximation
$$ -\log\gamma\approx 1-\gamma $$
Therefore,
$$ h \gtrsim \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \log \left( \frac{1}{(1-\gamma)\epsilon} \right)= \tilde{\mathcal{O}} \left( \frac{1}{1-\gamma} \right) $$
This tells us that the effective horizon of a discounted MDP is roughly
$$ \frac{1}{1-\gamma} $$
So even though the problem is infinite-horizon, discounting makes it behave like a long but finite-horizon problem.
4. Bellman Optimality in the Infinite-Horizon Case In the infinite-horizon discounted setting, the Bellman optimality equation becomes time-independent.
The optimal value satisfies
$$ V^\star(s)= \max_a \left( r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ V^\star(s’) \right] \right) $$
The optimal Q-function satisfies
$$ Q^\star(s,a)= r(s,a)+ \gamma E_{s’\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)} \left[ \max_{a’}Q^\star(s’,a’) \right] $$
Once $Q^\star$ is known, the optimal policy is simply
$$ \pi^\star(s)= \arg\max_a Q^\star(s,a) $$
This is the infinite-horizon version of the same idea:
value tells us which action is good, and the policy follows the action with the best value.
5. Summary This section connects value computation to policy optimization.
The core logic is:
$$ \text{Bellman equation}\rightarrow\text{value function}\rightarrow\text{policy improvement} $$
For finite-horizon problems, we can prove optimality by backward induction.
For known environments, we can solve the problem by planning, mainly through value iteration or policy iteration.
For infinite-horizon problems, discounting makes the return finite and introduces an effective horizon:
$$ H_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx \frac{1}{1-\gamma} $$
So the big picture is:
$$ \text{RL is not only about estimating value. It is about using value to act better.} $$
6. Application Here we briefly introduce a method that leverages the idea of learning a transition model to improve policy learning.
In previous sections, planning assumes that the transition model is known. However, in real RL scenarios, the true transition model is usually unknown. Dreamer addresses this problem by learning a latent world model from interaction data [4]. In a simplified view, Dreamer learns a latent dynamics model: $$ z_{t+1}\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid z_t,a_t) $$
where $z_t$ is a compact latent state learned from observations.
Once this model is learned, Dreamer can imagine future trajectories in latent space:
$$ z_t,a_t,\hat{r_t},z_{t+1},a_{t+1},\hat{r}_{t+1},\dots $$
Then the actor and critic are trained on these imagined futures. In this sense, Dreamer connects back to the planning idea discussed above: when the true transition model is unavailable, it learns a transition model and uses the imagined futures from this model to train the policy and value function.
The following figure shows the pipeline of the classic Dreamer algorithm. Later variants have extended this framework, but the core idea remains similar [4, 5, 6].

Available online: http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html
[2] Richard Bellman. Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press, 1957.
[3] Martin L. Puterman. Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming. Wiley, 1994.
[4] Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Jimmy Ba, and Mohammad Norouzi. Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination. ICLR, 2020.
[5] Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Mohammad Norouzi, and Jimmy Ba. Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models. ICLR, 2021.
[6] Danijar Hafner, Jurgis Pasukonis, Jimmy Ba, and Timothy Lillicrap. Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models. arXiv, 2023.
